citation.author: Ruffino, Paolo
citation.title: There is no cure: Paratexts as remediations of agency in Red Dead Redemption 2
citation.venue: Convergence: The International Journal of Research into New Media Technologies, 28(2), 345-358 (Special Issue: Politicizing Agency in Digital Play After Humanism). DOI: 10.1177/13548565221081062

discipline: Media and communication studies / game studies (paratext theory, affect theory, auto-ethnography)
thesis: Player-made YouTube videos about curing Arthur Morgan's tuberculosis function not as instrumental guides but as paratexts that 'remediate' (in Bolter & Grusin's double sense of reforming-upon and healing) a perceived loss of player agency; because RDR2 stages the illness as a consequence with no shown cause and no cure, it withdraws the control normally granted to the white, able-bodied male protagonist, and the paratexts try to restore that agency on two registers (narrative-as-navigable-database and environment-as-exploitable-gamespace) while conceding their own futility ('there is no cure') and re-instating a normative controlling subject that Ruffino then traces into COVID-19 visual culture.
sections: Introduction: a consequence with no actions (RDR2 premise, Arthur, the gang, the TB puzzle, the cure-paratext corpus)
Methodology: auto-ethnography and the performative potential of paratexts (retrospective, multi-text, self-implicating; Genette/Consalvo)
Agency on the narrative: the disembodied subject of interactive storytelling (YouTube thumbnails as threshold-paratexts)
Agency on the environment: prevention in gamespace (the Thomas Downes hypothesis; Doak1851 video)
Remediating a global pandemic (COVID-19 memes, virus visualizations, contagion curves, social-distancing/jogging infographics)
Conclusion (real and fictional respiratory infections enmeshed in the virtuality of gamespace; prevention's exclusionary normativity)
concepts: paratext (Genette's thresholds; performative/illocutionary force; non-ontological separation of text and paratext)
remediation (Bolter & Grusin; double sense: reform/restore-upon medium AND heal, from Latin remederi)
agency as affect of control (Owen) rather than causal efficacy
narrative agency vs environmental agency (the two sites of negotiation)
ludic/narrative agency (Joyce) and mechanical/fictional agency (Cole & Gillies)
illusion of agency in branching narrative (Stang; Smethurst & Craps)
'there is no cure' / tuberculosis as figure of an invisible, uncaused agent
gamespace (Wark; everywhere/nowhere; network flattening via Anikina/Munster)
affect / structure of feeling / mediation-over-representation (Anable, Massumi, Kember & Zylinska, Barad)
white, able-bodied normativity and the disposability of human/nonhuman others
attention economy and clickbait ('linking' collapsed into 'liking', Lovink)
disembodied vision / turning story-line into navigation (Wark)
readings: YouTube thumbnails as threshold-paratexts that promise unexplored forks/dialogues/actions never actually present in game or video, producing a disembodied navigating subject (examples: 'Arthur NEVER Dies and LIVES After The Ending', 'TB Cure secret outcome', 'Revisiting the Doctor', 'How to Avoid Getting Tuberculosis from Thomas Downes')

Doak1851's ~10-min video (30 Nov 2018, 2M+ views, 5,000+ comments) on the Thomas Downes hypothesis: exploiting the one-item-removal rule (grab horse lead) to keep Arthur masked while beating Downes; admitting the outcome likely cannot change
Attempts to kill Downes (3'07''-7'30'') producing two Downeses (dead + respawned) because the encounter cannot be skipped; Downes as expendable NPC, killable in countless ways
Environmental control read via Galloway's algorithmic 'nonlinear narrative', Kagen's 'straightening' the narrative, and Joyce/Cole-&-Gillies agency distinctions
Racialized disposability of NPCs linked to Nakamura (WoW gold-farmers) and Anikina/Munster network aesthetics

Pandemic coda: bat-soup meme (consequences with no actions), WHO virus image, Guardian contagion curve, social-distancing/jogging infographics (one modeled by a Gran Turismo aerodynamics developer) as remediations imagining an able-bodied white male subject of prevention; 'the Thomas Downeses' and 'running while black' (Petrzela)

game_elements.how_treated: The hinge of the whole argument: contracted in Saint Denis, not shown happening, incurable in 1899, makes Arthur slower and less able to heal via food/drink; a 'consequence with no actions' that withdraws player agency and triggers the cure-paratexts
game_elements.locus: Abstract; Introduction (the diagnosis in Saint Denis); 'a consequence with no actions'

game_elements.how_treated: All four alternative endings have Arthur die while severely affected by TB; the final act's dialogues and choices are defined by awareness of impending death; used to argue the game revokes control/destiny-agency
game_elements.locus: Introduction ('The game has four alternative endings, and in each of these Arthur dies')

game_elements.how_treated: Mandatory early debt-collection scene; Arthur beats a visibly sick farmer at close range; community-theorized infection point; cannot be skipped (Downes respawns if killed); the article's core case study for environmental agency
game_elements.locus: 'Agency on the environment: prevention in gamespace'

game_elements.how_treated: A special item that powers up Arthur and partially alleviates TB symptoms but does not cure the disease; evidence the game offers mitigation without cure
game_elements.locus: Introduction ('A special item in the game, the Owl Feather Trinket...')

game_elements.how_treated: The promised-but-denied control over the storyline imagined as navigable forks; read against Stang's analysis of surplus, illusory choice in The Walking Dead and Owen's 'affect of being in control'
game_elements.locus: 'Agency on the narrative: the disembodied subject of interactive storytelling'

game_elements.element: Open-world violence / Arthur's capacity to dominate the environment (honor-adjacent)
game_elements.how_treated: Pre-illness Arthur hunts animals and beats/robs anyone; 'the environment is his playground'; framed as the fantasy of control that RDR2 later revokes; the honor system itself is not analyzed as a formal mechanic
game_elements.locus: 'Agency on the environment' ('Arthur might not be in control of his destiny, but he is capable of exercising control over others')

game_elements.how_treated: RDR2 removes only one equipped item before a non-interactive scene; Doak1851 exploits this (grabbing the horse lead) to keep Arthur masked while beating Downes; a precise mechanical detail doing argumentative work about gamespace control

game_elements.element: NPC respawn and cutscene-triggered item stripping
game_elements.how_treated: Killing Downes yields a duplicated NPC (one dead, one alive); the fight cutscene strips equipped masks; used to show the environment's resistance to player will and the absurdity of the cure-attempts
game_elements.locus: 'Agency on the environment' (the four-minute attempt at killing Downes)

themes: agency as affect/illusion of control rather than causal power
invisibility of cause and the desire to render it visible/navigable
disposability of human and nonhuman others (NPCs, animals, landscape)
white, able-bodied normativity as the implicit subject of mastery
attention economy and clickbait as material conditions of paratexts
continuity of virtual and lived 'gamespace' under capitalist networks
chronic illness, mortality and fatalism in videogame representation
interlocutors: Lisa Nakamura (2009); Diane Carr (2014); De Wildt et al. (2020)
Sarah Kember & Joanna Zylinska (2012); Aubrey Anable (2018); Brian Massumi (2002); Karen Barad (2007)
Melanie Kagen (2020); Henry Jenkins (2006); Marie-Laure Ryan (2004); Daniel Muriel & Garry Crawford (2018)

debate_axis_positions.note: Sits toward scripted-constraint: RDR2 'contradicts the promises of control and continuous progression' (Muriel & Crawford), revokes the protagonist's agency, and kills Arthur in all four endings. But Ruffino reframes the axis: the salient constraint is the INVISIBILITY OF CAUSE (a consequence with no actions), and the agency at stake is an affective/ideological fantasy, not literal causal efficacy. The cure-paratexts are players refusing the constraint, yet even the refusal concedes it ('there is no cure') while restoring the controlling subject elsewhere.

Aligns with the issue's performative/post-humanist turn: paratexts are mediations and performances productive of affect, not mere representations; routed through Barad's representationalism-vs-performativity debate.

tensions: Auto-ethnographic generalizability: argument grounded in one self-identified white able-bodied male player's affect, then scaled to claims about 'contemporary digital culture' and a global pandemic (framed as hypothesis of a 'comparable affective structure', not demonstrated equivalence).
Scale asymmetry between fictional TB and real COVID-19 (author concedes case studies differ 'in nature, gravity and scale'); the analogy is illuminating rather than equivalent.
The honor system is not engaged as a formal feedback mechanic despite the article foregrounding Arthur's environmental violence as the 'fantasy of control'.

Clickbait vs sincere play: the analysis reads genuine affective investment into an attention-economy genre whose producers partly game engagement metrics (desire and awareness of impossibility held together).

Performativity vs representation: the framework wants videos to be performances/mediations more than representations, yet the close readings necessarily describe representational content (thumbnails, dialogue, scenes).
